q: You are taking a 10 m yacht from Lymington across the Channel to Cherbourg for the weekend. A crew member says a passage plan is only for ships. What is the position?
a: SOLAS V asks every vessel going to sea to plan
o: Only vessels over 24 m must plan a passage
Only boats on charter must file a plan
Only passages beyond 60 M need a plan
why: SOLAS Chapter V applies to all who go to sea, small craft included: weather, tides, the boat, the crew, dangers.

q: You are about to take a crew of four from Dartmouth to Guernsey, and your plan covers the items on the card. What else does SOLAS V expect you to have thought through?
a: Ports of refuge and what you do if it goes wrong
o: The menu for each meal and who cooks it
The marina's berth fees on arrival
The crew's passport numbers and nationality
why: SOLAS V: weather, tides, the boat's limits, the crew, the dangers — and a contingency plan with ports of refuge.

q: The purpose of this week is a relaxed family cruise with two young children aboard. Two plans fit tomorrow's weather: a 25 M daylight hop or an 80 M overnight crossing. Which do you choose?
a: The 25 M daylight hop, in by teatime
o: The 80 M crossing, to gain a day of sailing
The 80 M crossing, as the children will sleep
Either — the plan is the same for any crew
why: The purpose and the crew set the plan: a family cruise wants short, easy legs, not a night crossing.

q: You are setting two watches for an overnight passage with the crew on the card. How do you pair them?
a: Ana with Chris; you with Ben and Dana
o: Chris with Dana; Ana with Ben; you on call
Ana with Ben; you alone, the novices asleep
Ben with Chris; Ana with Dana; you on call
why: Each watch needs a leader who can handle the boat and the traffic at night: never two novices alone on deck.

fig.title: Crew for tonight
lines: Ben — a few nights as crew

q: You plan to round a headland to the west under engine. Your boat's numbers are on the card. How do you plan the rounding?
a: Time it for the fair stream — you can barely stem the foul
o: Any time — 4 kn still beats a 3.5 kn stream
Go at the foul stream, close in along the shore
Go at slack, then motor hard into the foul
why: 4 kn against 3.5 kn leaves 0.5 kn over the ground in a rough sea: plan the rounding for the fair stream.

fig.title: Your boat's limits
lines: Into a short head sea: about 4 kn

q: You are planning a day passage along the Brittany coast. What is your ETA?
You are leaving harbour to round a headland at slack water, before the stream there turns foul. When do you slip the lines?

fig.title: Rounding the headland
lines: Boat speed 5 kn through the water
Stream on the leg: 1 kn fair

q: You must pass a tidal race on your way to the next harbour, and two departure times work. Which do you plan?
a: 0500 — wind and stream go the same way in the race
o: 1100 — a stream against the wind flattens the sea
1100 — the later start gives the crew more rest
Either — at force 5 the race makes no difference
why: Wind against a spring stream in a race builds steep, breaking seas: time the race for wind with tide.

fig.title: Two departure times
lines: 0500: at the race 0800, wind with tide
1100: at the race 1400, wind against tide

q: Your crew of four want to sail tomorrow; the GRIB for the route is on the card. Which plan do you make?
a: Leave 0600, in about 1415, before it builds
o: Leave 1200, in about 2015, with the fresher wind
Leave 0900, in about 1715, as it reaches 20 kn
Leave 1800, in about 0215, ahead of the westerly
why: 45 ÷ 5.5 ≈ 8 h 11 min: from 0600 you are in by mid-afternoon; a GRIB shows no gusts, so keep a margin.

q: You are sailing east along this coast and decide to put in before the wind arrives. Which harbour is your port of refuge?
a: C — open at all tides and sheltered from the SW
o: A — the nearest, and the sill keeps out the sea
B — the biggest, with room to enter at any tide
A or B — whichever you reach first in daylight
why: Arriving at HW+4 misses A's sill (HW±2); B is open to the SW 6; C works at any tide and gives shelter.

q: Your track for tomorrow's leg crosses a military firing range. What goes into the plan?
a: A track outside the area, and a watch on the range channel
o: The track through it — yachts may pass at any time
The track through it at full speed, radar on
A stop at the edge until the safety boat waves you in
why: While firing, keep clear: route round the danger area or pass outside firing hours, and listen to the range.

fig.title: Range danger area
lines: Your track crosses it at about 1100

q: You will round this headland tonight. How do you plan the rounding?
a: Stand 5 M off, well outside the race
o: Pass 0.5 M off, on the inshore passage
Go through the race to keep the track short
Pass 2 M off, on the race's inner edge
why: Wind against a spring stream at night: the inshore passage is for settled weather, so give the race a wide berth.

q: The pilot book warns of dense pot buoys inside the 20 m line along your route, and you will pass there at night. What does your plan say?
a: Keep the track outside the 20 m line
o: Motor close inshore, where the pots end
Follow the 20 m line, as the pots mark it
Keep to the route — pot buoys are lit
why: Unlit pot buoys can't be seen at night and foul a propeller: route outside the area where they are laid.

q: Checking the route a crew member built on the plotter, you find WP3 sits exactly on the north cardinal you must round. What do you do?
a: Move WP3 into safe water a few cables N of the buoy
o: Leave it — the buoy is the best mark there is
Move WP3 into the gap a few cables S of the buoy
Leave it, but steer by hand on that leg
why: A waypoint on a mark invites hitting it at night on autopilot; put it in safe water — north of a north cardinal.

q: Both waypoints of tonight's leg are in deep water. Checking the leg between them on the chart, what do you find?
a: It crosses a 1.8 m patch — add a waypoint to clear it
o: Nothing — the waypoints are clear, so the leg is
It crosses a 1.8 m patch — fine with 2.1 m at LW
It needs a slower speed over the shallow part
why: Check the whole leg, not only its ends: 1.8 + 0.3 = 2.1 m at LW leaves 0.1 m under a 2.0 m keel.

q: Your plan should say when the light will lift above the horizon. When do you expect to see it?
why: You first see it at its dipping range, 16 M: 28 − 16 = 12 M to run at 6 kn = 2 h; 2300 + 2 h = 0100.

fig.title: Landfall light
lines: Dipping range at your eye: 16 M
At 2300 the light is 28 M ahead

q: At 2310 you see a light fine on the bow and time it as Fl(3) 15s. What do you do first?
a: Time it again and check your position against the plan
o: Take it as the 2300 light — close enough
Alter towards it for a closer look
Strike it from the plan — lights change
why: A light that doesn't match the plan's characteristic or bearing is a warning: re-time it and fix your position.

q: You are planning a calm-weather passage that may be all under engine. How far can you motor under your reserve rule?
The tank water tastes of the tank, so you carry bottled drinking water for the passage. How much do you take?
why: 5 crew × 2 L × 3 days (2 days at sea + 1 spare) = 30 L.

fig.title: Drinking water
lines: Allow 2 L per person per day

q: Your crew of six keep three watches of two, round the clock. Which watch has 2100–2400 tomorrow evening?
a: Watch C
o: Watch A
Watch B
Whoever is least tired
why: Eight 3-hour watches a day shared by three: the rota moves on, A B C A B C A B — so C has 2100 tomorrow.

q: Your crew of four stand two watches, 4 on and 4 off. Why does the rota split 1600–2000 into two short watches?
a: So the watches alternate and nobody has 0000–0400 every night
o: So the watch leaders can both eat with the crew at 1800
So the skipper can stand a two-hour watch on his own
So the change of watch falls at sunset every day
why: Seven watches a day, not six: the odd number moves the rota on, so the 0000–0400 alternates.

q: At 0300 the watch leader sees a ship 5 M off whose bearing has not changed for ten minutes. You are asleep. What should the watch leader do?
a: Call you now, as the orders say
o: Wait until she is 1 M off, then call you
Alter 90° to port and log it for the morning
Call her on VHF and let you sleep on
why: A steady bearing means risk of collision and a CPA near zero: the night orders say call the skipper.

fig.title: Skipper's night orders
lines: Call me: any ship with CPA under 1 M
Call me: any doubt at all

q: Your crew of five gather in the cockpit before an overnight passage. Besides the safety gear, what does your briefing cover?
a: The route, the watches, the weather and plan B
o: The marina's rules on arrival and the berth fees
Only the MOB drill — the rest they will pick up
The menu for each day and who washes up
why: A crew briefing gives the plan: route and timings, watch system, forecast, the alternatives and ports of refuge.

q: Tomorrow you sail from Brighton to Fécamp, in France, with the papers on the card. What must you sort out before you leave?
a: Extend the insurance to cover French waters
o: Nothing — these papers cover any passage
A French registration for the boat
A French radio licence for the VHF
why: Check the policy's cruising limits against the plan: 'UK waters only' does not cover a passage to France.

q: You are leaving for a two-day passage to the Scilly Isles. With whom do you leave the passage plan?
a: Someone ashore, with your ETA and when to call for help
o: Nobody — the AIS shows the coastguard where you are
The crew only — the copy lives at the chart table
The fuel berth, who will chase you if you are late
why: A float plan ashore — boat, crew, route, ETA, when to raise the alarm — starts a search if you don't arrive.

q: You plan an overnight passage with a force 5 on the beam. What do you plan for the first night's hot meal?
a: A one-pot stew cooked in harbour, just to reheat
o: Fresh pasta cooked at sea at about midnight
A roast in the oven, ready for the first watch
Nothing hot — cold food until you arrive
why: Cook ahead in harbour: one pot, one burner, a few minutes at sea; hot food keeps the watches going.

q: You have built the route on the plotter zoomed out to show the whole passage. Before you rely on it, what do you check?
a: Zoom in along every leg, or run the route check
o: Nothing — the plotter warns of every hazard
Only the total distance against the paper plan
That the route line shows in red on the screen
why: Zoomed out, a plotter hides rocks and shoals: check each leg at large scale or with its hazard check.

fig.title: Route on the plotter
lines: Built zoomed out to show it all
Two legs pass close to headlands

q: You are checking the route you typed into the plotter against your paper plan. What do you do?
a: Check WP3's lat/long against the chart — one is mistyped
o: Trust the plotter — it computes the great circle
Trust the paper — plotters round the distance
Average the two and log the difference
why: A leg that disagrees in distance and bearing means a mistyped waypoint: compare each lat/long with the chart.

q: The forecast is force 7 gusting 8. Your crew vote to sail anyway and say the decision is theirs. Whose decision is it?
a: Yours — the skipper answers for boat and crew
o: The crew's — a majority vote decides it
The owner's, if the owner is aboard
The marina's — they close the harbour
why: The skipper is responsible for boat and crew; force 7 gusting 8 is beyond the moderate conditions of the ticket.

q: You hold an IYT Yachtmaster Coastal certificate. A friend asks you to skipper this crossing. What do you say?
a: No — it takes you beyond 60 M offshore
o: Yes — the forecast is moderate, so it is fine
Yes — the Coastal covers any Med crossing
Yes, if you sail it in daylight only
why: Yachtmaster Coastal covers passages up to 60 M offshore in moderate conditions; 95 M off is beyond it.

q: Your night watch's only log entry is on the card. What should each hourly entry hold?
a: Time, log, course, position, wind and barometer
o: Time and a note that all is well on board
The position from the plotter, nothing else
The crew on watch and what they have seen
why: Hourly: time, log reading, course steered, position, wind, barometer — enough to run a DR if the GPS fails.

q: Overnight, everything runs on the plotter. Why does your watch leader still plot a position on the paper chart every hour?
a: To have a recent position if the electronics fail
o: Because a plotter position is not legal at sea
To check that the plotter's clock is right
Only to complete the logbook for the owner
why: If the GPS or the power fails, an hourly position on paper lets you run a DR from a known point.

q: At noon you check your progress against the plan. What does it tell you?
a: ETA 1637 — you need 6.0 kn to make it
o: ETA 1701 — you need 6.0 kn to make it
ETA 1637 — you need 5.5 kn to make it
ETA 1600 — you make it with no change
why: 24 ÷ 5.2 = 4.62 h = 4 h 37 min → 1637, too late; 24 M in the 4 h left needs 24 ÷ 4 = 6.0 kn.

fig.title: 1200 — progress check
lines: The stream turns foul there at 1600

q: It is 1400 and the situation is on the card. What do you do?
a: Turn for port C, as the plan says
o: Press on — you will be past it by 1436
Press on and decide again at 1500
Heave to and wait for the next fair stream
why: A decision point is set ashore, rested, with the tide worked out: at 1400 you are not past, so plan B.

fig.title: Decision point
lines: If not: plan B, port C

q: You are 5 M off the harbour you planned to reach before dark, and the situation is on the card. What do you decide?
a: Stand off in open water, rest by turns, enter at dawn
o: Go straight in — the sooner in, the sooner asleep
Enter now with the plotter zoomed right in
Anchor off the rocks at the entrance until dawn
why: Fatigue breeds mistakes: with sea room and a light offshore wind, waiting for daylight is the safe choice.

fig.title: 0200, approaching
lines: Unknown harbour, rocks at the entry

q: One of your crew is getting worse, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Bear away for the port of refuge and get them ashore
o: Carry on — the seasickness will pass once ashore
Send them to their bunk below and carry on
Heave to until they feel better, then carry on
why: Six hours unable to keep water down means dehydration: the near, downwind port gets them ashore soonest.

fig.title: 0400, on watch
lines: Crew sick for 6 h, keeps no water down

q: You come up to take over the watch at midnight, and this is what you find. What do you do?
a: Call them back for a proper handover first
o: Take over and read the log in the morning
Wake the skipper to ask about the ship
Take the helm and work it out yourself
why: A handover gives course, position, traffic, sails, weather and orders — before the off-going watch goes below.

fig.title: 0000, change of watch
lines: Ship's lights on the port bow
You haven't seen the plot or the log

q: On a night passage your navigator needs to read the chart below while you keep watch on deck. What light does the chart table use?
a: A dim red light
o: The bright saloon lights
A white head torch on full
The deck light through the hatch
why: Red light keeps the watch's night vision, which takes 20–30 minutes to come back after white light.

q: It is 0100 and two crew go to the mast to reef. One asks for the spreader lights. What do you tell them?
a: On for the job only, then off — it hides your lights
o: Leave them on all night so ships can see you
Never — reef by feel, with no light at all
Keep them on and switch off the tricolour
why: A deck light dazzles the watch and masks your navigation lights: use it only as long as the job needs.

fig.title: 0100, reefing
lines: Two crew go to the mast

q: You are writing the harness rule into your night orders. What does it say?
a: Clip on before you come up the companionway
o: Clip on once you are sitting in the cockpit
Clip on only when you go forward of the mast
Clip on only when the wind is over force 5
why: Clip on from below to a strong point by the hatch and stay clipped on: at night a person overboard is hard to find.

q: You come up at 0300 to check the watch, and this is what you see. What is wrong?
a: No lookout is kept — the leader must wake the crew
o: Nothing — the leader at the wheel is the lookout
The autopilot should be on so both can rest
The second crew should be in a bunk below
why: The watch leader's job: a proper lookout all round, astern included, the log kept, and the skipper called.

fig.title: 0300, on deck
lines: Second crew asleep in the cockpit
No-one has looked astern for 20 min

q: You must cross this traffic separation scheme to the north. What do you steer?
a: Heading 000°T, and let the stream carry you west
o: Head into the stream to make good 000°T
Head 045°T to run with the eastbound traffic
Steer straight for the waypoint beyond it
why: Rule 10: cross on a heading at right angles to the traffic flow, accepting the set — the quickest, clearest crossing.

q: You cross the scheme on a heading at right angles to the lanes. How long are you in it, and where do you come out?
a: 2 h 00 min, 3.0 M west of where you went in
o: 1 h 55 min, 3.0 M west of where you went in
2 h 00 min, 3.0 M east of where you went in
2 h 06 min, due north of where you went in
why: Across the lanes you make 5 kn: 10 M ÷ 5 = 2 h; the stream sets you 1.5 × 2 = 3.0 M west.

q: Halfway across the scheme, your crew suggest heaving to until there is a gap in the next lane. What do you do?
a: Keep crossing, slowing to pass astern of a ship
o: Heave to in the zone until a clear gap opens
Turn and follow the zone along to its end
Turn into the lane and join the traffic flow
why: Rule 10: a separation zone is entered only to cross it; adjust speed to pass astern rather than wait in it.

fig.title: Halfway across
lines: Crew: 'let's wait here for a gap'

q: Fog closes in as you approach a shipping lane you must cross. What do you do?
a: Stay out of the lane, in shallow water, until it lifts
o: Cross now, slowly, ready to stop for each ship
Run along the lane with the traffic, at speed
Cross now on radar, trusting AIS to show every ship
why: Ships keep up speed in fog and not all show on AIS; shallow water keeps big ships away until you can see.

fig.title: Fog
lines: Radar and AIS aboard, crew of four

q: Using the stream for each hour, what is your ETA at the end of the leg?

fig.title: Leg 24 M, depart 0800
lines: Stream along the track, each hour:

q: The wind has died and you are motor-sailing the last leg. Is your fuel enough under your own rule?
a: No — the leg uses about 23 L, leaving about 9 L
o: Yes — the leg uses about 17.5 L, leaving 14.5 L
Yes — the leg uses about 14 L, leaving 18 L
No — the leg uses about 35 L, more than aboard
why: Over the ground 6 − 1.5 = 4.5 kn; 30 ÷ 4.5 = 6 h 40 min × 3.5 L/h ≈ 23 L; 32 − 23 ≈ 9 L, under 10 L.

fig.title: Motor-sailing leg
lines: Leg 30 M, stream 1.5 kn foul all the way
Rule: arrive with 10 L or more

q: You plan an overnight passage to a harbour you want to enter at 0700. When do you leave?
Your destination marina has a sill. What is the latest time you can leave and still get in?
why: The sill shuts at HW+3 = 2020; 42 ÷ 6 = 7 h; 2020 − 7 h = 1320.

fig.title: Marina sill
lines: 42 M at 6 kn over the ground

q: You will arrive at an unfamiliar harbour at about 0200. When do you prepare the pilotage plan for the entry?
a: Before you leave, in daylight, rested
o: On the approach, once the lights are in sight
At the entrance, with the plotter zoomed in
Not at all — the leading lights show the way
why: A pilotage plan is made ahead and unhurried: bearings, lights, marks and dangers on a card for the cockpit.

q: You are taking a 12 m catamaran to a harbour dead upwind, with the numbers on the card. Which way gets you there sooner, and how long does it take?
a: Motor-sail direct — about 6 h 00 min
o: Tack under sail — about 7 h 28 min
Tack under sail — about 6 h 04 min
Tack under sail — about 4 h 17 min
why: Tacking through 110°: 30 ÷ cos 55° = 52.3 M ÷ 7 kn = 7 h 28 min; motor-sailing 30 M at 5 kn = 6 h 00 min.

fig.title: Catamaran, harbour 30 M upwind
lines: On the wind under sail: 7 kn

q: You are loading a 12 m charter catamaran for a week of island passages. The crew want every water tank, jerrycan and locker filled to the top. What do you say?
a: Load what the plan needs plus a margin — weight slows a cat
o: Fill everything — more aboard is always safer
Fill everything and stow it all in the bows
Fill everything — a cat carries weight easily
why: A catamaran loses speed, windward ability and bridge-deck clearance with weight: load for the plan, heavy items central.

q: You plan a 60 M day passage with the figures on the card. When does your plan say you arrive?
a: 2000 — only just before dark
o: 1634 — well before dark
1800 — well before dark
1657 — well before dark
why: Plan on the speed you really average: 60 ÷ 5 = 12 h; 0800 + 12 h = 2000, half an hour before sunset.

fig.title: 60 M along the coast
lines: Best speed in a breeze: 7 kn
Your average on past passages: 5 kn

q: Two tidal gates fit tomorrow's passage, as on the card. Which do you plan for?
a: The early gate — in by daylight, after an early night
o: The late gate — the crew sleep in and arrive rested
The late gate — you leave in daylight, so it is safer
Either — they are just the two tides of one day
why: A strange, rocky entry at 2330 with novices is the risk to avoid: an early night and a 0300 start bring you in at 1300.

fig.title: Two gates tomorrow
lines: Harbour new to you, rocks at the entry
Crew: you, a watch leader, two novices

q: Your passage must meet the fair stream at the headland and the marina's sill, as on the card. When do you leave?
why: Leave 0730: 12 ÷ 5 = 2 h 24 min → headland 0954, stream fair; 18 ÷ 6 = 3 h → marina 1254, sill open.

fig.title: Gate and sill
lines: Harbour to headland: 12 M at 5 kn
Headland to marina: 18 M at 6 kn

q: You must be at the gate at slack water, and the stream on the way turns during the leg. Working it hour by hour, when do you leave?
why: From 1000 to 1300 at 6.5 kn: 19.5 M; the other 6 M at 4 kn take 1 h 30 min before 1000 → leave 0830.

fig.title: To the gate: 25.5 M
lines: Be at the gate at slack: 1300
Boat speed 5 kn through the water

q: The tidal gate puts you round the headland at 0200, and the harbour beyond is to be entered in daylight. What is the most you can make over the ground and not arrive too early?
a: 5.4 kn
o: 6.8 kn
4.5 kn
6.0 kn
why: 0200 to 0700 is 5 h: 27 ÷ 5 = 5.4 kn. Any faster and you are off a strange entrance in the dark.

q: Tomorrow's window is on the card. What is the latest time you can leave under your own rule?
why: 54 ÷ 6 = 9 h; in by 1600, two hours before the force 7: 1600 − 9 h = 0700.

fig.title: Tomorrow's window
lines: Your rule: in 2 h before it builds

q: You hold a Yachtmaster Coastal and plan this crossing between two islands. Which route do you plan?
a: Route B — it keeps you within 60 M of land
o: Route A — 72 M is close enough to 60 M
Route A, if you cross the middle by day
Route A, as long as the forecast is moderate
why: The Coastal covers passages up to 60 M offshore: route B is never more than 38 M off, for 12 M more sailing.

fig.title: Two routes
lines: Route A, direct: 72 M from land midway
Route B, via the island: 38 M off at most

q: The owner of a 13 m yacht asks you, as a Yachtmaster Coastal, to take her on a 50 M coastal passage that runs through the night. Can you?
a: Yes — the Coastal covers day and night passages
o: No — the Coastal covers daylight passages only
Only with a second skipper aboard at night
Only if no leg is longer than 20 M
why: Yachtmaster Coastal: command up to 24 m, up to 60 M offshore, in moderate conditions, by day and by night.

q: It is 2200 and the wind is rising, so you decide to put in for the night. Which harbour do you plan for?
a: B — lit entrance, open at all tides
o: A — the nearest, so the least time out
A, with the plotter zoomed right in
A, anchoring off the rocks until dawn
why: A port of refuge must be safe to enter at the time you get there: at night that means a lit, clear entrance.

q: Fog is forecast for your landfall at dawn. Which harbour does your plan use if it comes?
a: B — in along the 10 m line and the buoyed channel
o: A — the plotter shows the gap in the rocks
A, slowing to 2 kn as you near the rocks
Either — with radar, fog changes nothing
why: Plan a fog alternative ahead: an approach you can follow by depth and buoys, not a gap between rocks you must see.

q: Tonight's leg can take the short channel inside the banks or go round them outside. Which does your plan take?
a: The outer route, round the lit cardinal
o: The inner channel, a torch on each buoy
The inner channel, on the plotter alone
The inner channel, at full speed to save time
why: At night unlit buoys can't be seen in time: 3 M more round a lit mark costs half an hour and takes the guesswork out.

q: Tonight's route runs past bays where the pilot book shows fish farms marked by yellow flashing lights. How does your plan treat them?
a: Pass well off — moorings reach out beyond the lights
o: Pass between the lights — they mark the way in
Pass close by — the cages are only at the lights
Ignore them — fish farms lie only inside harbours
why: Fish-farm cages are held by long moorings and lines: route well clear of the yellow lights, more so at night.

q: Your route crosses the approach to a busy commercial port, as on the card. What goes into the plan for this leg?
a: The VTS channel, a watch on it, a quick crossing
o: Nothing — VTS is there for the ships only
A call on 16 for permission to cross
A track down the channel on the buoys
why: Plan a listening watch on the port's channel and a quick crossing of the deep-water channel at right angles, clear of ships.

fig.title: Port approach
lines: VTS on VHF 12 for the port area
Ships to 300 m, ferries every hour

q: You can make this overnight passage on either of two nights, as on the card. Which do you choose?
a: Friday — the moon lights the sea, sails and deck
o: Tuesday — the dark makes ships' lights stand out
Tuesday — a dark night is a better lesson
Either — the moon makes no odds at sea
why: With novices, a moonlit night shows the sails, the sea and the horizon: plan a night passage by the moon when you can.

fig.title: Two nights to choose
lines: Tuesday: new moon, dark all night
Friday: full moon, up 2000 to dawn

q: Your plan lists when each light should come into view. When do you expect to see this one?
why: A weak light shows only at its nominal range, not its rising range: 24 − 8 = 16 M at 6 kn = 2 h 40 min → 0040.

fig.title: Light on the next headland
lines: Rising range at your eye: 16 M
6 kn over the ground, good visibility

q: You are setting the cross-track error alarm for tonight's leg. What limit do you set?
why: The alarm must sound well before you reach danger: with the shoal 0.4 M off the track, set it inside that, about 0.2 M.

q: The plotter's route check reports no hazards on tonight's route. Looking at its settings, what do you do?
a: Widen the corridor past your XTE limit and run it again
o: Trust it — the check found no hazard
Narrow the corridor to make it stricter
Switch off the XTE alarm for leg 3
why: A check only looks inside its corridor: at 0.03 M it misses a reef 0.2 M off that your 0.25 M XTE limit lets you reach.

fig.title: Route check: no hazards
lines: Leg 3 passes 0.2 M off a reef

q: You let the plotter's auto-route build tomorrow's route, with the settings on the card. Before you trust it, what do you do?
a: Set the true draft and safety depth, then check each leg
o: Nothing — auto-routing works from the chart
Add 0.6 m to each depth in your head
Use it as it is, but by daylight only
why: Auto-routing knows only what it is told: with 1.5 m set for a 2.1 m keel it will route over water too shallow.

fig.title: Auto-route settings
lines: Draft: 1.5 m (set by the last owner)

q: For the passage home you reverse yesterday's route on the plotter. What do you check before you rely on it?
a: Each leg again — the dangers, marks and tide differ
o: Nothing — the same legs, just sailed the other way
Only that the waypoints run in the right order
Only the total distance against the outbound
why: A reversed route meets marks from the other side, turns in new places and other streams: plan and check it afresh.

q: At 0200 the plotter dies, as on the card. What lets you carry on safely?
a: The paper plan: courses, distances, lights for each leg
o: The plotter's last screen, from memory
The marina's phone number at the destination
The ETA you gave your shore contact
why: The written plan and the paper chart let you keep a DR and pick up the next light when the electronics fail.

fig.title: 0200 — plotter dark
lines: Power fine, the unit has failed
Next turn in 6 M, rocks to port

q: Fuel is short for this calm leg in your catamaran. Which way do you motor, and what does the leg take?
a: One engine — about 33 L for the leg
o: Both engines — about 46 L for the leg
Both engines — about 23 L for the leg
One engine — about 28 L for the leg
why: One engine: 60 ÷ 5.5 = 10.9 h × 3.0 = 33 L; both: 60 ÷ 6.5 = 9.2 h × 5.0 = 46 L. Slower on one saves 13 L.

q: Before a few days among islands with no fuel berth, you check the tank against the plan on the card. Is it enough?
a: Yes — about 39 L used, 21 L left
o: Yes — about 30 L used, 30 L left
No — about 48 L used, 12 L left
No — about 54 L used, 6 L left
why: Motoring 10 × 3 = 30 L, charging 3 × 2 h × 1.5 = 9 L: 39 L used, 21 L left — above the 15 L reserve.

fig.title: Fuel for the trip
lines: Tank 60 L, full; keep 15 L in reserve
Motoring on passage: 10 h at 3 L/h
3 days at anchor: charge 2 h a day

q: Your crew of six will be away from water for a while, as on the card. What daily allowance per person do you set?
why: Keep a day spare: 300 L ÷ (6 crew × 5 days) = 10 L each a day. Their shore habit of 15 L would need 450 L.

fig.title: Water
lines: Tank 300 L, full; crew of six
Ashore they use about 15 L each a day

q: A lively first night is forecast for your crew of six. What do you stow by the companionway before you leave?
a: Snacks, water and a flask, within reach of the watch
o: Nothing — meals will be cooked to order below
The week's tins, to help the boat's trim
Fresh fruit only, stowed in the forepeak
why: In a seaway the watch needs food and drink it can reach without cooking: ready snacks and a hot flask by the hatch.

q: You are sailing from Kos across to the Turkish coast, and the pilot book extract is on the card. Where does your plan make the first stop?
a: Harbour A, Q flag up, to clear in first
o: Bay B for the night, clearing in tomorrow
Bay B, as long as nobody goes ashore
Either — clear in by phone once you arrive
why: Arriving from another country, the first stop is a port of entry to clear customs and immigration, under the Q flag.

fig.title: Pilot book
lines: Harbour A: port of entry — customs, police
Bay B: 5 M closer, anchorage only

q: For the return passage two more crew join you, as on the card. How many hours on deck does each person now stand in 24 h?
a: 8 h
o: 6 h
why: Three watches of two on 4-hour watches: six watches a day, two each, 2 × 4 = 8 h on deck — down from 12 h.

fig.title: Watches
lines: Out: crew of 4, two watches, 4 on 4 off
Back: crew of 6, three watches of two
Watches still 4 hours, round the clock

q: With a crew of four you set the night watches as on the card. Why stagger them like this?
a: Someone on deck has always seen the last two hours
o: So each crew member sleeps eight hours at once
So the skipper never needs to be called
So two fresh crew can take over together
why: Staggered watches: one person changes every 2 h, so the deck always has someone who knows the traffic and the weather.

fig.title: Staggered watches
lines: Each stands 4 h; one changes every 2 h

q: With a crew of six on a two-night passage, you keep yourself out of the watch rota. Why?
a: To be rested for the landfall and on call at any hour
o: Because a skipper never stands a watch
So the crew learn without help all night
Because the skipper may not steer at sea
why: A skipper outside the rota sleeps when possible and comes fresh to the decisions, the traffic and the arrival.

q: You and one friend take a 10 m yacht on a 70 M overnight passage. How do you plan the night?
a: Alternate 3-hour watches; the one off sleeps below
o: Both stay on deck all night together
You stay up all night while your friend sleeps
Both sleep, with radar and AIS alarms set
why: Two-handed, one keeps the watch while the other sleeps from the start: short watches, and never both asleep.

q: At the briefing, a novice asks why she needs to know the ports of refuge and plan B. What do you tell her?
a: If I am hurt, the crew must get in or call for help
o: She doesn't — only the watch leaders need it
It keeps her busy while she is off watch
The law asks every crew member to sign it
why: The skipper can be the casualty: every crew member should know the route, the refuges and how to call for help.

q: Your navigator prepared tonight's passage plan. At 2300 you find one of its waypoints on a shoal. Who answers for the plan?
a: You — the skipper checks and owns the plan
o: The navigator who drew it up
The maker of the plotter's charts
Whoever is on watch at the time
why: Planning can be delegated, responsibility cannot: the skipper checks the plan and answers for the boat and crew.

q: At 0300 your watch leader sees the light abeam fade out, as on the card. What should she do?
a: Call you — the visibility is closing in
o: Log it as a failed light and carry on
Carry on — you have left its sector
Swap the lookout — his eyes are tired
why: A light that fades well inside its range means falling visibility: the night orders say call the skipper.

fig.title: Night orders
lines: Call me if visibility drops below 2 M
It is well inside its nominal range

q: The autopilot is following the route through the night, as on the card. What do your night orders say about WP5?
a: Call me before WP5; the watch confirms the turn
o: Nothing — the autopilot turns there by itself
Let the plotter skip WP5 to save time
Turn at WP5 only if the plotter beeps
why: At an auto-advancing waypoint the boat turns on its own: the watch checks the new heading is safe before it does.

fig.title: Tonight on autopilot
lines: The route advances at each waypoint
WP5 at about 0330: turn 70° to port
Next leg passes 0.5 M off rocks

q: At 0215 you tack and put in a reef, between the hourly entries on the card. What goes in the log?
a: An entry now: time, log, new course, the reef
o: Nothing until the 0300 hourly entry
The reef only — the course is on the plotter
A note in the morning once all is calm
why: Log each change as it happens — course, sails, a fix, an event — so a DR can be run from the latest entry.

q: The plotter shows your ETA, as on the card. When do you really expect to arrive?
why: To 1200 at 7 kn: 14 M; the last 16 M at 5.5 − 1.5 = 4 kn take 4 h → 1600. The plotter assumes today's SOG holds.

fig.title: 1000 — 30 M to go
lines: Then foul 1.5 kn to the end

q: You are sailing for a tidal gate and falling behind the plan. What is the latest time you can start the engine and still make it?
why: Sailing all 6 h makes 27 M, 3 M short; the engine gains 2 kn, so you need 1.5 h of it: 1600 − 1:30 = 1430.

fig.title: 1000 — behind the plan
lines: 30 M to the gate; it shuts at 1600

q: You reach the headland three hours late, just as the stream turns against you. If you push on, when are you through?
why: To 2100 at 5 − 4 = 1 kn: 6 M; the last 2 M at 9 kn take 13 min → 2113. Waiting at anchor for 2100 gets you through by 2153.

fig.title: 1500 — at the headland, late
lines: 8 M of strong stream to clear
Foul 4 kn until 2100, then fair 4 kn
Boat 5 kn under engine, calm sea

q: At 0300 your engine fails, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Sail to the anchorage and anchor under sail
o: Carry on to the marina and decide at the gap
Call MAYDAY for a tow into the marina
Sail into the marina and drop sails inside
why: Plan B must fit the boat you now have: an open anchorage downwind that you can sail into, not a tight entry.

fig.title: 0300 — engine dead
lines: It will not restart; no stream to worry
Marina: narrow entry, no room to sail

q: A new forecast comes in on passage, as on the card. What do you decide?
a: Bear away for the port of refuge now
o: Press on — you will be in before it builds
Press on and reef when it reaches force 7
Heave to until the stronger wind has passed
why: 30 M at 4 kn made good is 7.5 h, and the force 7 arrives in 6 h: a reach to shelter 12 M away is your plan B.

fig.title: New forecast
lines: Destination 30 M upwind, 4 kn made good
Port of refuge 12 M on a reach
It is sheltered from the SW

q: On the first night two of your six crew are out of action, as on the card. How do you re-form the watches?
a: Two watches of two, each led by Ana or Ben
o: Keep three watches; Tom and Eva stand theirs
Four watches of one, an hour each, Kim too
No watches — all four on deck until dawn
why: Fewer crew, fewer watches — but each still needs an experienced leader: Ana with Kim, Ben with you.

fig.title: Night 1, 2200
lines: Eva: hand injury, can't steer or winch

q: You have diverted to your plan B port, as on the card. What do you do as soon as you are in?
a: Call your shore contact with the new port
o: Nothing — you are safe, so no alarm will come
Call them tomorrow once the plan is final
Call the coastguard to close the passage
why: A float plan works only if it is kept up to date: tell your contact where you are before the alarm time.

fig.title: Plan B port, 1900
lines: Shore contact: alarm if no word by 2000
You planned to be in port A at 1700
Now safe in port C, phone signal good

q: A crew member feeling queasy on passage wants to lie down in the forepeak bunk. Where do you send them instead?
a: On deck in fresh air, or a bunk low and amidships
o: The forepeak — it is the quietest place aboard
The chart table, to keep busy with the plot
The galley, to cook a big hot meal
why: The motion is worst forward and high: fresh air and the horizon on deck, or a low bunk amidships, ease seasickness.

q: Handing over at 0200, the off-going leader tells you what is on the card. What is missing?
a: Your position and the next waypoint or turn
o: The name of the ship on the port bow
The engine hours since you left
The time of breakfast for the morning
why: A handover gives the position and the next turn, as well as course, traffic, sails, weather and the skipper's orders.

fig.title: 0200 handover
lines: Ship on the port bow, bearing drawing aft
Skipper: call at 0400 or if in doubt

q: At 0300 the jib sheet fouls on the foredeck. You and one other are on watch. How do you go forward?
a: Tell your watch mate, clip on, go while they watch you
o: Slip forward quietly without telling anyone
Unclip to move fast, clip on again at the bow
Go with no torch so as to keep night vision
why: At night nobody goes forward unseen: say so, clip on to the jackstay, and have the helm watch you all the way.

q: You plan to cross a shipping lane at right angles, as on the card. How far does a ship in the lane travel while you cross it?
why: 4 M at 5 kn = 48 min = 0.8 h; 18 kn × 0.8 h = 14.4 M. A ship still out of sight can reach you before you are across.

q: Halfway across a traffic lane, fog shuts in, as on the card. What do you do?
a: Hold the heading across, radar watch, fog signals
o: Turn back to the side you came from
Stop in the lane until the fog lifts
Turn and run with the traffic flow
why: Halfway across, the quickest way out is ahead: keep the right-angle heading at safe speed, plot on radar, sound signals.

fig.title: Fog in the lane
lines: Radar on; AIS shows two ships 6 M E

q: Your harbour is dead upwind, with the figures on the card. Which makes more progress towards it?
a: Motor-sail 30° off — about 5.2 kn made good
o: Motor straight at it — 4.5 kn made good
Motor-sail 30° off — about 6.0 kn made good
Motor-sail 30° off — about 3.0 kn made good
why: Made good towards the harbour: 6.0 × cos 30° = 5.2 kn, more than the 4.5 kn punching straight into the chop.

fig.title: Harbour dead upwind
lines: Force 4 and a short, steep chop

q: The wind dies at 2200 with the harbour still ahead, as on the card. At which speed do you motor?
a: 5 kn — off the entrance at 0600, 12 L left
o: 6 kn — off the entrance at 0440, 9 L left
6 kn — off the entrance at 0440, 15 L left
5 kn — off the entrance at 0600, 4 L left
why: 6 kn: 6 h 40 min × 3.2 = 21 L, 9 L left, in the dark. 5 kn: 8 h × 2.2 = 18 L, 12 L left, at first light.

fig.title: 2200 — wind gone
lines: Fuel 30 L; keep 10 L in reserve
